title: What to Include on a Checklist for New Bookkeeping Clients
summary: Onboarding a new bookkeeping client? Use this checklist to collect documents, complete key setup steps, and learn client onboarding best practices from Intuit.

- What to Include on a Checklist for New Bookkeeping Clients


A standardized onboarding process can help you build trust and rapport with your bookkeeping clients and keep them coming back. A thorough checklist covers the essentials, including intake, data setup, systems and security, reconciliation, and training. It should be simple for your team to follow, helping you avoid unnecessary back-and-forth and delays.


Here’s a look at what to include in each section of your bookkeeping onboarding checklist, plus how a consistent process can help as your practice grows.


## **Key Points**


- Your bookkeeping client onboarding checklist should include client intake, account setup, systems and permissions, initial reconciliation, and training.
- A repeatable checklist helps your team avoid missed steps and extra work while giving every client a more consistent experience.
- Accounting conferences like Intuit Connect can help you learn strategies for streamlining operations and scaling your practice.


## **Client Intake and Preparation**


A smooth onboarding process starts with gathering the right information and setting clear expectations. These steps can help you get the engagement off to an organized start and prepare for the setup work ahead.


### **Finalize the Service Agreement/Contract**


Onboarding a new bookkeeping client typically begins with a signed contract. It should clearly spell out the services and terms of engagement, along with pricing and timelines. Besides covering your legal bases, the goal is to get everyone on the same page from the get-go.


### **Collect Business and Financial Information**


Gather the records you’ll need to get a clear picture of the client’s business and set up their books. Depending on the engagement, this may include:


- **Business information:** Legal business name, contact information, industry, ownership details, customer and vendor information, payroll reports, and insurance information
- **Financial information:** Current and prior financial records, bank and credit card information, revenue sources, invoices, tax filings, and past ledgers
- **Tax and compliance information:** Tax ID numbers and filing requirements, partnership agreements, permits and licenses, relevant tax documents, and reporting schedules


### **Send a Welcome Message and Next Steps**


Help your client understand what happens next by setting up a welcome sequence early on. Your welcome package can include:


- A personalized greeting or welcome message (e.g., an email or video)
- A digital packet with an overview of the onboarding process and guidelines
- Requests for any missing or supporting documentation, if needed
- A prompt for next steps, such as logging into their client portal
- Their assigned onboarding lead or point of contact


A welcome sequence keeps the lines of communication open and shows that your practice is organized and committed to providing the best service possible.


## **Data and Account Setup**


Once you have the basics, you can start gathering the financial data and account access you need to set up the client’s books. A standardized document request can make this process easier to repeat across clients and help your team keep track of what’s still outstanding.


### **Send a Standardized Document Request**


In your accounting onboarding checklist, create a standardized document request form. This makes it a lot easier to set up and configure new accounts. It also cuts down on the confusion that can come with juggling several clients at once.


Depending on the engagement, you might ask for:


- Accounts receivable and accounts payable (AP/AR) records
- Active loan agreements
- Previous financial statements
- Tax records and relevant tax IDs
- Bank and payment account information


You can use these records to review the client’s existing chart of accounts or build one that fits their business. **** The chart typically organizes the client’s assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, and expenses, but the specific accounts will vary by client and industry.


### **Connect Accounts and Confirm Settings**


Identify the accounting, banking, and payment platforms the client uses and arrange the appropriate access and permissions. Confirm important settings, including the client’s fiscal year. Also, determine what financial data needs to be connected or migrated.


### **Set Up a Secure Way to Share Information**


Make sure clients know how to communicate with you and securely share financial information. If you use a client portal, walk them through how to upload and e-sign documents, send messages, sync accounts, make payments, or update their information.


## **Systems, Permissions, and Security**


[Accounting technology](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/accounting-technology/) can make it easier for you and your team to collaborate and manage client work. But setting up the right systems is only part of the process. You’ll also need to decide who has access to what and how you’ll protect sensitive client information.


### **Set Up User Roles and Permissions**


Decide which team members and clients need access to each system, then assign permissions based on what they need to do. Limiting access to what’s necessary helps protect sensitive information while clarifying roles and responsibilities.


### **Put Security Measures in Place**


Review how your firm will securely store and access client information. Depending on your systems and security policies, that may include:


- Password managers
- Multifactor authentication (MFA)
- Encrypted client portals
- Other safeguards for handling sensitive data


For more guidance on protecting sensitive client information, review the[IRS’s security recommendations for tax professionals](https://www.irs.gov/identity-theft-central/identity-theft-information-for-tax-professionals) .


### **Confirm Data Backup and Retention Policies**


Make sure you have processes for backing up client data and retaining records for the appropriate amount of time.


## **Initial Reconciliation and Validation**


Verifying new client data before officially entering it into the system is crucial. If you don’t, you risk both operational integrity and financial inaccuracy, not to mention potential compliance issues.


## **Confirm Opening Balances**


As part of the onboarding process, cross-reference the new client’s opening balances with their historical records to make sure everything adds up. This might involve reviewing different accounts, such as bank and credit card statements. Be prepared to check their assets and liabilities, as well as claimed equity.


### **Review the Trial Balance**


You may want to run an initial[trial balance](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/r/accounting/trial-balance/) . This is simply an internal report listing each account’s closing balance. Look for unexpected balances or other discrepancies that may need further investigation before moving forward.


Start by choosing a specific cutoff date. Depending on when the client comes in, this might be the end of the most recent month or fiscal year. Use that date as the baseline for all future accounting.


### **Spot-Check Transaction Categorization**


Review a sample of historical transactions to see how they’ve been categorized. If you find inconsistencies or questionable entries, address them before using the same approach with new transactions.


## **Client Training and Handover**


The final phase of your bookkeeping client onboarding checklist is the client walkthrough. You might cover this in a meeting or share the information through email or a client portal. However you go about it, keep the process consistent and give clients a clear place to find the information they need.


### **Walk the Client Through Your Process**


Give clients the guidance they need to work with you confidently. Depending on your services and systems, your walkthrough may cover:


- Training materials or documentation
- Scope of work and expectations
- Logins and upload procedures
- Billing processes
- Rules of engagement
- Best communication methods


### **Set a Schedule for Ongoing Communication**


At this point, your client should be fairly set up. Still, set up a[regular communication schedule](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/global/resources/accountants/guide-to-client-communication-for-accountants/) even after onboarding is complete. This could be monthly or quarterly (or on another schedule that works for the engagement). And be sure to send updates about internal changes that might affect them, like a new point of contact or system migration.


### **Ask for Feedback**


Give new clients the opportunity to provide feedback about your process. Even if they’re not fully satisfied, you can use that feedback to make improvements as you[grow your accounting firm](https://www.intuit.com/blog/innovative-thinking/accounting-firm-growth-strategy/) .


## **Why a Standardized Checklist Helps You Scale**


Accounting and advisory firms can lose clients for all kinds of reasons, and a frustrating onboarding experience can set the relationship off on the wrong foot. A clear, repeatable process helps you provide a more consistent experience as your client base grows.


A bookkeeping client onboarding checklist can also cut down on rework and back-and-forth. And that can make it easier for your team to onboard more clients without reinventing the process each time.

## **FAQs**


###


The access levels and permissions needed for bookkeeping work depend heavily on the system. For example, you typically only need a standard user or accountant-level role when using software like QuickBooks Online. For bank and credit card accounts, a read-only transaction feed might be sufficient. If you’re talking client portals or document systems, you’ll get full access to your financial documents and history, though control is usually shared.


###


Email isn’t exactly safe when it comes to sending and receiving confidential financial documents or data. So, instead, use a secure client portal where they can access their own info or safely communicate with your team.


###


Your timeline will depend on the client and complexity of the engagement, but setting target dates can help keep onboarding moving. For example, you might aim to collect key documents within 5 business days and complete the full bookkeeping client onboarding checklist within 2 weeks. Build in extra time for missing records, account access, or other issues that could delay the process.
